contributions.headingText: Colloid adenocarcinoma is an invasive adenocarcinoma where extensive pools of extracellular mucin distend alveolar spaces and destroy alveolar walls, up to the complete effacement of underlying lung parenchyma.
2C25.Z & XH7GY6 Malignant neoplasms of bronchus or lung, unspecified & Adenocarcinoma of lung, mucinous
Not recommended: mucinous cystadenocarcinoma; mucinous cystic tumour of borderline malignancy.
Most tumours occur in the peripheral lung parenchyma {15087663}.
These are commonly incidentally detected localized masses on imaging {27220284}.
The epidemiology is similar to that of other adenocarcinomas.
The etiology is similar to that of other adenocarcinomas.

Because gastrointestinal differentiation would be responsible for pathogenesis of mucinous tumours of the lung, its pathogenesis may overlap with that of mucinous/colloid gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma where most mucin is extracellularly accumulated.

Tumours are variably circumscribed, unencapsulated, solitary, soft, gelatinous nodules, which are mucoid in appearance and bulging on cut surface. Tumour size ranges from 5 to 100 mm {1369799; 25776025}. Uncommonly, these tumours may appear markedly cystic.

Colloid adenocarcinoma shows abundant extracellular mucin in pools, which distend alveolar spaces and destroy their walls, showing an overtly invasive growth pattern into the alveolar spaces. Mucin deposits enlarge and dissect through the lung parenchyma, creating pools of mucin-rich matrix. The tumour cells are mucin-laden cuboidal to tall columnar cells, sometimes exhibiting signet-ring morphology. They can float in mucin pools or focally line residual alveolar walls or fibrous tissue surrounding mucin pools {28451462}. Tumour cells can be inconspicuous and well differentiated, making diagnosis difficult, particularly in small biopsies and frozen sections. They may show pseudostratification and cytological atypia; however, typically the mitotic count is low and necrosis is absent. An inflammatory infiltrate with histiocytes and a giant cell reaction to the mucin may be seen. The extremely rare tumours previously classified as mucinous cystadenocarcinoma are now included in colloid adenocarcinoma.

Immunohistochemistry

Colloid adenocarcinoma exhibits admixed intestinal markers (CDX2, MUC2, CK20). However, colloid adenocarcinomas are also consistently CK7-positive. Staining for TTF1, napsin A, and EMA (MUC1) is either negative or weak and focal {28451462; 15087663; 24651909}.

Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis comprises metastases of mucinous carcinoma from other organs, including the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, and breast. For lung primary tumours, invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma generally shows preserved alveolar walls lacking the large pools of mucin destroying alveolar walls characteristic of colloid adenocarcinoma. Although colloid adenocarcinoma is rarely mixed with other adenocarcinoma subtypes, ≥ 50% of the tumour should have this appearance to warrant the diagnosis of colloid adenocarcinoma.
A predominant background of extracellular mucin contains scant mucin-laden tumour cells, isolated or in small clustered aggregates, usually with bland cytological features.

About one half of tumours show KRAS mutations {31634654; 28451462; 28255028}, with molecular similarities to invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung and mucin-producing gastrointestinal and pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms {28451462; 28255028; 24604757}. Other frequently detected mutations are in STK11 and PARP1 {31634654}.

Essential:

  • Abundant pools of extracellular mucin that distend alveolar spaces and destroy their walls
  • Tumour cells are mucin-filled, cuboidal to columnar, and either floating within the mucin pools or lining fibrous walls of mucin-filled spaces
  • ≥ 50% colloid pattern when mixed with other adenocarcinoma subtypes
  • Distinction from metastases from the other organs

Desirable:

  • Bland cytology of tumour cells in mucin pools
  • Frequent positivity for CK7 and CDX2

Staging should be performed according to the eighth-edition TNM classification [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017.]].

The clinical course is mostly indolent, with a relatively favourable prognosis after complete surgical resection. The presence of signet-ring cells and a non-colloid component signifies worse prognosis, with recurrence and metastasis {15087663}. Colloid adenocarcinomas are generally negative for predictive biomarkers such as EGFR mutation and ALK rearrangement {25776025; 26450556}.
